title: Caring for kesh
hook: washing, combing and covering the hair as daily care

segments.voice: Yesterday, why a written code: it travels, it settles things fairly, it welcomes the newcomer. Your line was one code, many homes.

Early morning in a Sikh home. Someone sits on the edge of a bed, long hair down past the shoulders, still damp. A small wooden comb works through it from the ends up, one knot at a time. Then the hair is twisted, wound into a knot on top of the head, and covered. Outside that room, people mostly notice only the last step. Early on this path you met kesh, uncut hair kept as it was made, one of the five Ks. Today isn't the rule. It's the morning.
screen: `DAMP HAIR, A WOODEN COMB.` → `TWISTED, KNOTTED, COVERED.` → `NOT THE RULE: THE MORNING.`

segments.voice: The Sikh code asks Sikhs to keep the hair uncut, and Sikhs speak of it as a gift kept as it was given. But keeping is a verb, and it has three parts. Washing comes first. Long hair is washed and dried with care, often as part of the early-morning bath before prayer, so the body is clean when the mind turns to the Name. Combing comes second. The kangha, the small comb, is itself one of the five Ks, kept in the hair so it can be used any time of day. The code asks Sikhs to comb the hair, and some say a prayer or recite while they comb, so tending the hair and remembering God happen together. Covering comes third. The hair is gathered up and covered, with a turban, a keski, a chunni or another covering, kept clean and kept in honor. Notice what this does to a rule. Don't cut your hair could be kept by doing nothing at all. Caring for kesh asks for something every single morning. It turns a boundary into a small daily act of attention, and the body into part of the practice. A Sikh doesn't only keep the hair; the hair keeps reminding the Sikh. Each tangle asks for patience. Each covering is a small act of respect. And tomorrow the comb comes out again.
screen: `KEEPING IS A VERB.` · `WASHED BEFORE PRAYER.` · `COMBED WITH THE KANGHA.` · `COVERED, KEPT IN HONOR.` · then, large: `DAILY CARE.`

segments.voice: If a comb or brush is nearby, pick it up; if your hair is short or gone, use your fingers instead. Work slowly from the ends up, and when you meet a knot, don't pull: pause, and work it loose. If you pray, remember God with each stroke; if not, just give your hands your full attention.
Caring for kesh. Washing, combing and covering the uncut hair, as a daily act of care and remembrance. Today's word.
Your line: daily care. A rule that's kept by doing, every morning. Go gently.

No. It means cutting it only on festival days, then letting it grow back.
chat.meaning: Keeping is a verb: caring for kesh means washing, combing and covering it every morning, a small daily act of attention.

notes: 'The code asks Sikhs to comb the hair' is stated without a number; the Sikh Rehat Maryada's wording on combing (some renderings say twice a day) should be confirmed before any number is added.
The early-morning bath before prayer is described as common ('often'); the code's guidance on rising early and bathing supports the habit, but please confirm or soften.
'Sikhs speak of it as a gift kept as it was given' is a general description; confirm.
Head coverings listed: turban, keski, chunni; confirm the list and that it is appropriate for all genders as phrased.
